topic.title: How airlines really make money (it isn't the seats)

title: How airlines really make money (it isn't the seats)
description:
You think an airline sells seats. Its most valuable product is the points on your credit card.
Rohan books a flight and follows his money: the thin profit on the seat, the fare ladder, the fees, the cargo under his feet, the miles banks buy by the billion, and the loyalty programme that can be worth more than the airline itself.
Then the question nobody asks: who actually pays for all those free flights?

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:22 The seat
1:00 The fare ladder
2:05 The fees
3:17 The cargo
4:17 The miles
6:03 The bank inside

lines.text: Rohan just paid $400 for this flight. The airline's profit on his seat? About $12. The real money went somewhere else: through his card, and into a bank.
Hold on. That little? Then why does every airline keep begging me to sign up for its credit card?
Six ways an airline makes money. The seat. The fare ladder. The fees. The cargo under your feet. The miles. And the last one, the bank hiding inside the airline.
And by the end, you'll know who really pays for every free flight. Hint: it might be you.
Way one. The seat.
Start with the ticket. Rohan paid $400 for one seat on one flight.
Out of that fare comes the fuel, the crew's pay, the airport fees and the plane itself.
Fuel alone can eat around a quarter of an airline's costs, and no airline controls the price of oil.
After all of it, an airline keeps about 3% of the fare as profit. On Rohan's ticket, that's $12.
That's about the price of a sandwich at the gate.
Airlines run on thin margins. One bad year of fuel prices, a strike or a storm season, and the profit is simply gone.
Warren Buffett once joked that a smart investor at Kitty Hawk should have shot the first plane down.
So why run an airline at all? Because the seat isn't really the product. It's the doorway.
And not every seat sells for $400. The woman beside Rohan paid far less, for the very same seat.
Way two. The fare ladder.
Way two starts at the departures board. One flight, and a whole ladder of prices.
Priya booked this flight months ahead. She paid $160.
Rohan booked last week, for the seat right beside hers. His fare: $400.
That's $240 more for the identical trip. Rohan's fare is 2.5× hers.
I paid more than double for the exact same seat? Next to her?
Airlines sell every flight in buckets. The cheapest bucket sells out first, then the next, and the price of every bucket keeps climbing.
Software watches every booking. When seats sell fast, the price jumps. When they sell slowly, a sale appears.
So the price I pay depends on when I happen to look?
And on how badly you need to go. The system can't read your mind, but it can read the calendar.
Before the software, a ticket had one price on a paper coupon. Now one flight can carry dozens of prices at once.
Fly on a quiet Tuesday instead of a busy Friday, and the very same seat can cost less.
Who buys the top bucket? People who must fly: business trips, family emergencies, plans made the night before.
School holidays, a festival, a big game in town: the moment demand jumps, every bucket climbs with it.
The cheap seats fill the plane. The expensive ones pay for it.
That's why I book early. The cheap bucket is built for people who plan.
But the fare is only the price you see up front. The next way waits for Rohan at the check-in desk.
Way three. The fees.
At the desk, Rohan's suitcase costs extra. So does a seat with legroom, and the snack on board.
On the cheapest tickets, even sitting next to your own family can cost extra.
I have to pay to sit next to my own mother?
Say his extras add $60 to the trip. That's $48 more than the airline's profit on his whole seat.
Fees aren't pure profit. But a bag in a hold that's flying anyway costs the airline far less than it charges.
The ticket is the bait, my friend. The extras are the meal.
When did bags stop flying for free? I remember when they just did.
In America, around the time fuel prices spiked. The fuel came down. The bag fees stayed.
Airlines call it unbundling. The low fare gets you through the door. Everything else is sold piece by piece.
Airlines in America collect billions of dollars a year from bag fees alone.
The very cheapest tickets often come with the fewest rights: no seat choice, no changes, sometimes not even a big cabin bag.
And if Rohan's plans change, the cheapest fare may not let him change a thing. He buys a whole new ticket.
And the scramble for overhead space? Plenty of people are just dodging the checked-bag fee.
That's why the fare on the first screen is the least useful number. The whole trip is the real one.
Add it all up, and Rohan's bargain fare is not much of a bargain any more.
Bag after bag, flight after flight, those little fees pile into a mountain.
So the cheap fare was never the real price. Got it.
Three ways so far: the seat, the fare and the fees. All small. The next one is riding right under Rohan's feet.
Way four. The cargo.
Three ways are on the board. The fourth is hiding under the floor of the plane.
Below the cabin floor is the hold. Next to the suitcases ride crates, parcels and sacks of mail.
A big passenger jet can carry tons of freight below the cabin, on almost every trip it flies.
Companies pay to ship their goods on a plane that was flying that route anyway.
Take one full flight: 200 seats at $400 is $80,000 of fares. Say cargo adds another 10% on top. That's $8,000.
In the pandemic, some airlines flew planes with no passengers at all. Only cargo.
When nobody could travel, the parcels kept some of those planes in the air.
Post offices pay airlines to carry mail, too. A letter sent abroad often rides in the hold of a passenger flight.
Online shopping made it bigger. A phone ordered tonight on the other side of the world can fly under passengers within days.
So my suitcase shares a ride with someone's online shopping.
A parcel's day: the warehouse, the airport, the hold under Rohan's seat, and a doorstep on the other side of the world within days.
Cargo is quiet money. Nobody posts about a parcel's flight.
Every empty corner of the hold is space the airline can sell, on a trip it was making anyway.
Four ways down, and none of them is the big one. The big one is sitting in Rohan's wallet.
Way five. The miles.
Every flight earns Rohan miles. Here's the strange part: the airline can create as many miles as it likes.
In effect, an airline prints its own money. And then it sells that money to banks.
A bank buys miles by the billion, to hand out on the airline's credit card.
And not only to banks. Airlines sell miles to hotels, car rental firms and shops: anyone who wants to reward a customer.
Why would a bank pay for miles? Because miles make people swipe, and every swipe pays the bank.
Each time Rohan pays with the card, the shop pays a swipe fee: an assumed 2% of the bill.
He spends $2,000 a month on the card. That's $40 of swipe fees every month, and $480 a year, from just one card.
Part of that fee comes back to Rohan as miles. The rest stays with the bank, which bought those miles from the airline.
And that's one shopper. Now multiply him by millions of cardholders.
Banks buy the miles, and the miles bring them customers. Customers who swipe and swipe.
One of America's biggest airlines reports getting billions of dollars a year from its card partner. Not from flights. From a bank.
Banks often pay the airline extra for every new cardholder who signs up. That's why the crew sometimes walk the aisle with card offers.
That's why they keep begging me to sign up. It was never about the flight.
So when I swipe for groceries, an airline gets paid?
Through the bank, yes. Your weekly shop is part of the airline business now.
And many miles are never spent at all. They expire, or sit forgotten in old accounts. The industry has a word for it: breakage.
A mile sold and never spent is money the airline never has to give back in seats.
A mile costs the airline very little to create. It only costs a seat when someone spends it, often a seat that would have flown empty.
The airline can also change what a mile buys. Ask for more miles for the same seat, and everyone's miles quietly shrink.
So my miles are a currency the airline can shrink whenever it wants?
Like any currency. Except this one has one central bank, and it's the airline.
Year one, Rohan's swipes send $480 through the system. Year five, the same again. After 10 years, $4,800, from one ordinary shopper.
So that's five ways: seats, fares, fees, cargo and miles. But someone has to pay for all those free flights. The last way shows who.
Way six. The bank inside the airline.
Five ways so far, all lined up. Before the sixth, Rohan has a question.
Fine. Then who's paying for all these free flights?
Here's the twist. Those free flights aren't free. The shop pays the swipe fee, then builds it into its prices, for everyone. Even the people paying cash.
Shops don't swallow that fee. They price it in. Groceries, coffee, fuel: a little higher for everyone.
Economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston found that people paying cash end up helping fund card rewards.
And the fancier the card, the bigger the swipe fee the shop usually pays on it.
And anyone who carries a balance pays interest, often far more than the rewards they earn.
So the people paying for my free flight might be the ones who can least afford it.
That doesn't make the card a scam. It means the rewards are paid for. Just not always by the person earning them.
The winners: people who pay in full and actually use the perks. The losers: people who pay interest, and people who pay cash.
Now follow all of those payments. The swipe fees, the sign-ups, the annual fees. They flow into one place: the loyalty programme.
That loyalty programme is where Rohan's miles live. Its members, its card deals and its partners are a business of their own.
The bank pays for the miles. The airline keeps the cash. And the members keep chasing their next free flight.
In the pandemic, with planes parked, big American airlines borrowed billions of dollars, and put up their loyalty programmes as security.
And the lenders valued those programmes at more than the whole airline was worth on the stock market.
Think about that. The whole company, planes and all, was valued at less than its points.
So it's a bank. With some planes attached.
The plane is the shop window. The loyalty programme is the bank behind it.
In a bad year, the planes lose money. People still swipe their cards.
And Rohan pays to belong to that bank. His premium card charges an annual fee of $550.
Over 10 years, that's $5,500 in fees alone, before he books a single seat.
Lounge visits, a free bag, a companion ticket. Each perk is only worth something if Rohan actually uses it.
But I get lounge access and a free checked bag!
If you use them, they can be worth it. Lots of people pay for perks they never touch.
So once a year, I do the sum: what did the card give me, and what did it cost me?
And if the perks don't beat the fee, about the same money, $45 a month, invested at an assumed 7%, could grow to $55,219 in 30 years.
So Rohan makes one rule. The card is cash: he pays it off in full, every single month. That way the miles are his, and the interest is nobody's.
Six ways to make money, and only one of them actually flies you anywhere.
Simplified maths with assumed margins, fees and returns. Would you still take the airline card? Comment below.
